who-this-is-for.text: This page is for somebody who wants to witness that a name is free and get their deposit back, somebody who wants to book one, and somebody holding a live name who wants to change where it receives payments, recover after losing the current control key, or end it permanently. Ending a name needs the committed recovery key or the retirement quorum, and the active witness moves into completion-only custody before it burns.

change-the-payment-destination.text: The controller may set, replace, or clear one optional payment destination. The destination is routing data, not authority. The sequence keeps the registry identity, key, representative, controller, next commitment, and quorum unchanged, and makes no registry request, mint, or burn. Wrong authority, multiple destinations, and control-field tampering are refused.

recover-with-the-committed-next-controll.text: Recovery reveals the complete next controller address, checks its canonical bytes against the domain-separated BLAKE two b two hundred and fifty six commitment, and requires its payment-key signer. The old controller need not sign. The successor keeps the representative, installs the revealed controller, and stores a fresh commitment. Only canonical base and enterprise payment-key addresses are supported.

retire-permanently.text: Ending a name needs the committed recovery key or the retirement quorum, never the current control key alone. A thief who has taken the everyday control key and the holder themselves look identical to the chain, so if the current key could end a name the thief could end it, and recovery would arrive too late because there would be nothing left to recover. The recovery key is the one thing the thief does not have. The authorized transaction moves the active witness into completion-only custody, mints the terminating approval on the same proof, and creates the completion request beside it; anyone may then fold that request, and the name's byte becomes terminal forever. A terminal name is not a deleted name: its key stays in the map, and the one request it still admits is the read.

consumer-and-ledger-boundary.text: The consumer contract is source-bound to a pinned cardano KERI commit. It uses Conway inline-datum and required-signer precedents without importing KERI schemas or claiming compiled-script interoperability. Singular publishes its own wire indices and field order, binds one registry identity per application, and rejects a rival initialization seed. The table separates what existing tooling constrains, what Singular publishes, and what remains outside the candidate.

evidence-and-release-status.text: The browser drives pending-claim cancellation, maintenance, recovery, and both retirement routes with their refusals. Retirement is queued first, showing pending, and completed by a separate permissionless fold, showing retired or Over. The reconciliation binds all forty-three model and corpus identities to public controls and assertions. The downloadable archive carries raw model, contract, scenarios, replay sources, pinned tooling, and exact identities under one SHA two hundred and fifty six manifest. This is still an unaccepted design candidate, not a deployed validator or ledger observation.

how-a-name-moves-in-the-registry.text: Naming is an instance of the registry, not a layer bolted beside it. A name is one key in the registry's authenticated map whose value is a single byte — absent, active or terminal — and seven requests move a key, each one moving a witness token that is what a reader looks at, never the root. The naming walkthrough states the state table, the seven requests and the four witness laws once; this page uses them without repeating them. Two things are naming's own. Ending a name needs the committed recovery key or the retirement quorum, and never the current control key alone. And no application script runs at fold time: the naming validator certifies an edge in advance by minting one approval whose asset name binds the edge, the key, the owner and the destination, and the registry recomputes that name from the request itself and refuses anything that does not match. A folder can be anyone, which is exactly why the destination is bound: without it a folder could route your name to itself.

book-a-name.text: A booking has no separate claim to stage first and no Withdraw edge to cancel one with. It is two things, an approval and a request, and the request waits until someone folds it. Alice mints one approval whose asset name binds the edge, the key, herself as owner, and the destination — the application's own address with the hash of the datum her record will carry. Minting it needs her signature, and that is the only signature anybody ever checks for this booking. She attaches it to a registry request and lets go. Whoever folds the batch next creates her record at the address she bound, with the datum she bound, carrying the active witness and the deposit her request rode with, less the folder's tip.

witness-that-a-name-is-free.text: Carol does not want a name; she wants to say that nobody has one. She mints an absence approval, which needs no signature from anyone, names her own address as the refund, and submits a request with a deposit. The fold puts the absent witness into the cage's own custody with the key and Carol's refund address recorded beside it. Whoever books the name afterwards spends that custody, and the fold pays Carol's deposit back to the address she named. If nobody books it, Carol takes her own witness back: that deletion is certified by the refund address the custody recorded, and by nobody else.
